draft.title: Statistical claims
card: A statistical claim is only as good as the data behind it. Ask who collected the data, how they collected it and how many people or items it covers.

Check who is in the sample. If it leaves out part of the group the claim is about, or only includes people who chose to reply, the result may be biased. A very small sample can also give a result that does not hold for the whole group.
Check the numbers. A percentage with no sample size can mislead, because 90% of 10 people is only 9 people. Ask if the report says how many were asked.
Check the conclusion. A link between two things does not prove one caused the other. A result also only applies to the group that was sampled, not to a wider group.
draft.remember: Before trusting a claim, check who collected the data, how big and fair the sample was, and whether the conclusion goes too far.

a.q: A news article says 80% of shoppers prefer a store's brand. The store asked 5 people at its own checkout. Why is the claim weak?
opts: The sample is tiny and likely to favour the shop's brand
The sample is tiny, but 80% of 5 people is not possible
The sample is fair, but 80% is too high a result to trust
The sample is fair, but the result needs a graph to count
a.why: Five people already buying at the checkout is a tiny sample that is likely to favour the brand. The arithmetic is fine, since 80% of 5 is 4 people. A high percentage is not a fault by itself, and a claim does not need a graph to count.
a.clue: Ask whether the sample is large enough and whether it was chosen fairly.

b.q: An online article says teens who sleep more get better marks, so sleep causes high marks. The survey only showed a link. What is wrong?
opts: A link alone does not show that sleep caused the marks
The survey is too fair to show any link at all
Marks cannot be compared with hours of sleep
The article should have used a larger graph
b.why: Two things can happen together without one causing the other. Another factor, such as routine, may affect both. Marks and sleep can be compared, and the size of a graph does not decide if a cause is shown.
b.clue: Ask if the data shows a link only, or proves a cause.

a.best: The sample is tiny and likely to favour the shop's brand

b.best: A link alone does not show that sleep caused the marks

proposal.title: Questioning statistical claims
card: A statistical claim is only as good as the data behind it. Ask who collected the data, how they collected it and how many people or items it covers.

Check who is in the sample. If it leaves out part of the group the claim is about, or only includes people who chose to reply, the result may be biased. A very small sample can also give a result that does not hold for the whole group.
Check the numbers. A percentage with no sample size can mislead, because 90% of 10 people is only 9 people. Ask if the report says how many were asked.

Check the conclusion. A link means two things tend to happen together, but it does not prove one caused the other, as another factor may cause both. A result may also not hold for a wider group that was not sampled.

b.q: A survey of 2000 Year 10 students, chosen at random from schools across Australia, found those who slept more had higher marks. A headline says "More sleep causes better marks". What is the main problem?
opts: It treats a link as proof that sleep causes better marks
A sample of 2000 students is too small to show a link
It gives a percentage without saying the sample size
Only students who chose to reply were in the sample
b.why: The survey shows that more sleep and higher marks tend to go together, but that does not prove sleep caused the marks. Another factor, such as a steady routine, may affect both. The sample is large and chosen at random, so its size and fairness are not the problem.
b.clue: The sample looks fine. Look at what the headline concludes.
